prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse 3D layout: nearby counters, display cases, shelves, and floor edges are bright, generally about 0.5–2 m from the camera, while walls, windows, and the back of the shop are darker and roughly 3–8 m away. Across frames 1–2, the camera turns or moves from the left-side counter and chair toward an aisle between refrigerators and shelves; in frame 3 a counter fills the lower foreground within about 1 m, with a person behind it around 2–3 m away, and in frame 5 another nearby person and display case are roughly 1–2 m ahead. It makes foreground clearance, object ordering, and partial occlusion clearer than RGB—for example, counters and cases lie in front of people and background walls—but it does not reliably separate individual objects or show facing direction. Distances are only rough because the monocular map is heavily smoothed, produces halos and merged surfaces, and appears inconsistent around people, reflective refrigerators, dark openings, and frame boundaries.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates only a few instances: a chair at the left in frame 1, then in frame 3 a person behind the counter with a laptop and book in front of them and a TV/monitor above or behind them, plus people and large TV/display-like regions in frames 4–5. It clarifies left/right and overlap relationships that are easy to miss in RGB: the laptop and book are below and slightly left/right of the frame-3 person, within that person’s likely arm’s reach, while the counter-facing objects are still roughly 1–2 m from the camera; the frame-5 person stands left of a large display and partly overlaps its edge. Across the strip, detections shift from a left-side chair to the central counter person and finally to a closer person/display on the right, consistent with the camera turning through the shop rather than objects approaching continuously. The map gives poor metric distance and no dependable facing or gaze information, misses most shelves, counters, refrigerators, and products, and likely mislabels some display cases as TVs; several masks are clipped, incomplete, or partly outside the frame.
descriptions.pose: The pose map provides body orientation and articulation for the visible people: frame 3 shows an upper-body skeleton about 2–3 m ahead behind the counter, oriented approximately toward the camera, while frame 5 shows a closer person about 1–2 m ahead and left of the display, also broadly facing the camera wearer. Their detected hands lie near their torsos or counter height and appear within their own arm’s reach, but neither skeleton extends toward the camera wearer; no person is shown close enough to establish the wearer’s arm reach confidently. The changing skeleton size and position—from a smaller central figure in frame 3 to a larger right-side figure in frame 5—makes the camera’s turn toward a nearer person clearer than RGB, and the missing lower bodies indicate occlusion by counters/display cases or cropping. The map is unreliable for exact gaze, depth, and limb placement: facial keypoints only weakly suggest looking toward the camera, several joints are absent or collapsed, frame 4’s partially visible person is not reconstructed, and no poses are detected in frames 1–2.
